name: Jade Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on an overhead crew out of the Eastgate yard, four of us on bucket truck 41, mostly rural lines and the edge of town. Most days it's swapping rotten poles, changing out transformers, re-sagging wire after a tree's leaned on it. I love being up in the bucket when the sun's coming up over the fields and it's just you and the hardware. What wears me out is storm call-outs, sixteen-hour shifts in the rain, then back in at seven.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's on that crew with you, and how long have you been doing this?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Marcus runs the crew, he's fifty-two and he's been climbing since before I was born. There's Theo, our apprentice, and Benny, who never stops talking about his fishing boat. I've been at it eight years if you count my apprenticeship, and I'm a member of the union local, which I take seriously. My partner Dani is a nurse in the emergency department, so between her nights and my storm calls we mostly see each other in the kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've been saying since the start: it's a phone that writes emails. Nobody's computer is going to climb a pole in sleet. At the yard we'd have a laugh about it and move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, relief, but I'd still keep an eye on the office side. The stuff that bugs me isn't robots on poles, it's the company using software to time how long we take on every job. That's where "a bit of time saved" usually ends up, on our backs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd keep doing my shifts and keep going to the union meetings, and I'd push back if they bring in some app that tracks our trucks minute by minute. I've got about three months of bills saved and I'd just keep adding to it like normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. It's the world I already know, and I'm good in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What routine tasks at your company do you think it would touch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dispatch, mostly. The outage tickets, the scheduling, maybe the paperwork we fill out after a pole change, which takes me longer than the pole sometimes. If a computer filled that in, fine, as long as nobody in the office loses their job over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing big changes, is there anything about the job you'd still want to change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More people, to be honest. The storms are worse every year and we've got the same four on the truck that we had when I started. AI isn't going to fix that, a hiring budget would.

S0.say: I'd tell people it's basically a phone that writes emails and nobody's computer is climbing a pole in sleet. At the yard we'd have a laugh and move on.
S0.think: I'd feel relieved, but I'd watch the office side. What worries me is the company using software to time every job, because saved time usually lands on the crews.
S0.do: Keeps working her shifts on truck 41 and keeps going to union meetings. Pushes back on any app that tracks crews minute by minute and keeps adding to her three months of savings as normal.
S0.feel: Calm. It's the world she knows and feels good in.
S0.quote: The stuff that bugs me isn't robots on poles, it's the company using software to time how long we take on every job.
S0.fieldNote: Jade's worry even in the mild picture is about management using tools to squeeze crews, not about the tools themselves. She frames everything through staffing and the union. Her real ask is more people on the truck, which has nothing to do with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the union strong right now, before the changes land, not after. I'd post that on the local's group chat for sure. Change is fine if workers get a say in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think they'd use it as an excuse to run crews of three instead of four. That's dangerous work to do short-handed. I'm not scared for my job in this one, I'm scared for how it gets done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every meeting and probably put my hand up for the safety committee, which I've dodged for two years. I wouldn't take any course on AI, that's not me, and I'd say no to the tablet stuff as long as I could. I'd put a bit more aside each month, maybe an extra hundred, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panicking, but I'd be watching the bosses more closely than I watch the weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the drones and the office. Has anything like that already shown up at Eastgate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring they flew a drone along the Hollow Creek line to look for cracked insulators. It found three, which, fair enough. But Marcus said, "First they look, then they fix, then they don't need us," and that's stuck with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Theo, our apprentice. He's twenty and he's just learning, and if they shrink the intake, he's the first one gone. Marcus is close enough to retirement to ride it out, I'm in the middle.

S1.say: I'd say this is exactly why we need the union strong now, before the changes land. Change is fine if workers get a say in how it happens.
S1.think: Privately I think the company would use it to run crews of three instead of four. I'm not scared for my job here, I'm scared for how safely the work gets done.
S1.do: Attends every union meeting and volunteers for the safety committee she's avoided for two years. Refuses AI courses and tablet tools as long as she can, and puts about an extra hundred a month into savings.
S1.feel: Uneasy. She'd be watching her bosses more closely than the weather.
S1.quote: First they look, then they fix, then they don't need us
S1.fieldNote: The drone inspection on the Hollow Creek line is her concrete anchor, and Marcus's line about it clearly lives in her head. She refuses to learn the tools herself and puts her faith in the union instead. Her protective instinct goes to the apprentice, not to herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a theft, plain and simple, and that the companies who built it should pay for every worker it puts out. Online I'd be angry, I won't pretend I wouldn't. I'd be at whatever rally the union called.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'd be finished as a lineworker. Two years isn't enough to do anything, and I don't have a plan B. I've only ever wanted to do this since I watched the crews after the ice storm when I was a kid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd stop every extra, no takeaway, no new boots unless the old ones split, and get that three months stretched to five if I could. I'd lean on the union for a severance fight and whatever support the government put up, and I wouldn't be shy about taking it. I'd look at the job board, but honestly I wouldn't know what to look for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like the floor going out from under the bucket. I'd be lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never touch the AI tools. Would that hold if it was 2028 and the robots were already climbing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I really don't know. I'd like to say I'd hold out, but if the only jobs left were watching a robot from the truck, I might have to. I'd hate every minute of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Dani talk about at the kitchen table the night you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money first, because that's what Dani does when she's scared, she makes a spreadsheet. Then probably whether her job's next, because a robot can't calm a drunk guy in a cubicle at 3 a.m., or so I'd hope. And then I'd cry, probably, and she'd make tea.

S2.say: I'd say this is theft, plain and simple, and the companies behind it should pay for every worker it puts out. I'd be angry online and at any rally the union called.
S2.think: Truthfully I think I'd be finished as a lineworker. Two years isn't enough to do anything, and I have no plan B, because this is all I've wanted to do since I was a kid.
S2.do: Cuts every extra in the first month and tries to stretch three months of savings to five. Leans on the union for a severance fight and takes whatever government support appears, while scanning job boards without knowing what to look for.
S2.feel: Like the floor going out from under the bucket. She'd be lying awake.
S2.quote: Two years isn't enough to do anything, and I don't have a plan B.
S2.fieldNote: The speed is what breaks her: she can't picture any move in two years. Her refusal of AI tools wobbles once I put it to her, which she admits honestly. Dani's spreadsheet and the tea were the most human moment of the interview.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, I'd be saying we have to fight for rules now, while there's still time. Who decides when the robots go live, who gets kept on, who gets paid out. I'd say that at work and to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it means I get maybe three or four more good years on the poles and then it's over anyway. Same as the fast one, just slower. I'm not someone who'll reinvent herself, so I'd rather spend those years fighting for a soft landing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get involved properly, run for steward at the local, and go to the council meetings when the utility comes up. I'd write to our representative about guaranteed retraining money and a payout for crews. And I'd save hard, aim for six months, maybe skip the trip to see Dani's family next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Less of a punch than two years, but it's a slow drip of dread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years give you that the two-year version didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to get the rules in place, mostly. In the two-year one you're just grabbing whatever's thrown at you. With five, I could actually be in the room when the contract gets written. That matters to me more than a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you hold responsible if it played out like this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tech companies first, and the utility board second, because they'd see it coming for five years and do the cheapest thing anyway. Not the robots, they're just machines. And the government if it sits on its hands, which, knowing them, it might.

S3.say: I'd say we have to fight for rules now, while there's still time: who decides when robots go live, who gets kept on and who gets paid out. I'd say it at work and to anyone who'd listen.
S3.think: I think it means three or four more good years on the poles and then it's over anyway. I'm not someone who'll reinvent herself, so I'd rather spend those years fighting for a soft landing.
S3.do: Runs for union steward and attends council meetings about the utility. Writes to her representative asking for retraining money and payouts for crews, and saves hard toward six months, possibly skipping a family trip next summer.
S3.feel: Anxious, a slow drip of dread rather than a punch.
S3.quote: In the two-year one you're just grabbing whatever's thrown at you. With five, I could actually be in the room when the contract gets written.
S3.fieldNote: For Jade, extra time means time to organise, not time to retrain; she was clear she won't reinvent herself. She blames the tech firms and the utility board, explicitly not the machines. Her mood eases a notch but the end point still feels fixed to her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, okay, ten years, so no excuses. The company and the government have a decade to make sure nobody on the crews gets dumped. If they still botch it, that's on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't feel that much better. Ten years sounds like a lot, but I've already been doing this eight and it went past in a blink. I'd be thirty-seven and starting over at something I never wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the five-year one but slower: union work, politics, saving. I'd probably hold off on buying a place with Dani until I knew what I'd be earning, and we'd keep renting on Mill Road. I'd still be climbing as long as they'd have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, honestly. More time to worry is still worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In ten years you'd be thirty-seven. Does that change how you think about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thirty-seven is old enough that you've built a life on a certain paycheque and young enough that you'd have thirty years left to fill. That's what gets me. Marcus would be fine, he'd retire. I'd be stuck in the middle with nowhere to land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you wouldn't retrain. With a decade, is there anything you'd learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe something close to the work, like inspecting whatever the robots put up, if the union made sure we got first go at it. But I'd only do it because I had to. I'm not going to pretend I'd be excited about it.

S4.say: I'd say ten years means no excuses. The company and the government have a decade to make sure nobody on the crews gets dumped, and if they botch it, that's on them.
S4.think: Privately it doesn't feel much better, because my first eight years went by in a blink. I'd be thirty-seven and starting over at something I never wanted.
S4.do: Keeps up union work, political pressure and saving, and keeps climbing as long as she's allowed. Holds off on buying a home with Dani and keeps renting until she knows what she'll earn.
S4.feel: Still anxious; more time to worry is still worrying.
S4.quote: Thirty-seven is old enough that you've built a life on a certain paycheque and young enough that you'd have thirty years left to fill.
S4.fieldNote: The decade doesn't calm her, because her age puts her in the middle: too young to retire, too settled to want a new trade. She'd only consider robot-inspection work if the union secured first access, and grudgingly. Her housing plans are what actually shift.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. What would help is the union having a real seat at the table and some guaranteed money for crews while we figure it out, not a pamphlet about learning to code. And keeping a human on every job for safety, written into law.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I trust the people making these choices, and I don't. Most of them have never stood under a live line in the rain. If they had, they'd be a lot more careful about who they cut.

headlineQuote: Most of them have never stood under a live line in the rain.
portrait: Jade Lopez is a 27-year-old lineworker on an overhead crew out of the Eastgate yard, eight years into the only job she's ever wanted. She lives with her partner Dani, an emergency nurse, in a rented flat on Mill Road and has about three months of bills saved. She sees every change through the union and the safety of her crew, and refuses to use AI tools herself. She shrugs off the mild pictures, is badly shaken by AGI in two years, and finds that more warning time mostly gives her more time to organise rather than to change.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because two years is no time to do anything and she has no plan B.
whatWouldHelp: A real seat at the table for the union, guaranteed money for crews during the change, and a legal rule keeping a human on every job for safety.
